stem: A 76-year-old woman has 2 days of left lower abdominal pain, fever and vomiting. Her white count is 22,500/mm³ with many bands, and CT shows an abscess from a ruptured sigmoid diverticulum. Neutrophils are recruited and switched on by bacterial products such as lipopolysaccharide binding to receptors on their surface.
oneliner: 76F + ruptured sigmoid diverticulum abscess + fever + WBC 22,500 with bands + neutrophils sense bacterial LPS → which receptor family?
ask: Neutrophils sense the bacterial products mainly through which type of receptor?

whyNot.B: Inside the cell: **steroids, thyroid hormone, vitamin D**
whyNot.C: Fast transmitters such as **acetylcholine at the nicotinic receptor**
whyNot.E: Found on **T cells**, not neutrophils, and needs MHC-presented peptide

answer: Toll-like receptors (pattern-recognition receptors, e.g. TLR4 for LPS)
why: Innate cells recognise **conserved microbial patterns (PAMPs)** with **Toll-like receptors**: **TLR4 + CD14 bind LPS** of Gram-negative bacteria and switch on **NF-κB** → cytokines.
chain: Binds CD14 + TLR4 on neutrophils and macrophages
Fever, neutrophilia, neutrophils move to the abscess

idea.rule: Innate immunity = pattern recognition (TLRs) on fixed receptors; adaptive = specific antigen receptors (TCR, BCR).
also: TLR2: Gram-positive lipoteichoic acid
TLR3, 7, 8: viral RNA; TLR9: unmethylated CpG DNA
TLR5: flagellin

stem: A 28-year-old man who migrated from rural Central America has had 2 weeks of headache, vomiting, and blurred vision, and had a generalized seizure today. Both optic discs are swollen. MRI shows a cystic lesion with a small bright dot inside it, in the right lateral ventricle. The right lateral ventricle is markedly enlarged, and the left lateral, third, and fourth ventricles are normal in size.
oneliner: 28M + migrant, rural Central America + headache, vomiting, blurred vision + seizure + papilledema + cyst with dot in right lateral ventricle + only right lateral ventricle large; left, 3rd, 4th normal → where is CSF flow blocked?
ask: At which site is the CSF flow most likely obstructed?

whyNot.A: Aqueduct block enlarges **both lateral and third** ventricles; the third is normal
whyNot.B: Fourth-ventricle outlet block enlarges the **fourth ventricle** too
whyNot.D: Would enlarge the **left** lateral ventricle; the **left is normal**

answer: Cyst blocking the right foramen of Monro (neurocysticercosis)
why: **Only one lateral ventricle is enlarged** while the others are normal, so the block is **at that ventricle's foramen of Monro**. A **Taenia solium cyst with a scolex** (the dot) lodges there, trapping CSF upstream and raising **intracranial pressure** (headache, papilledema).
chain: Cyst in the right lateral ventricle
CSF trapped in the right ventricle

idea.rule: The pattern of ventricular enlargement locates the block: one ventricle, foramen of Monro; lateral plus third, aqueduct.
also: Neurocysticercosis is the commonest cause of adult-onset seizures in endemic regions
Treat with albendazole plus steroids, with antiepileptics
Caused by ingesting T. solium eggs

stem: A 41-year-old man recently released from prison has had 3 months of cough, night sweats and weight loss. His tuberculin skin test is 14 mm and a chest x-ray shows upper-lobe lesions. A lung biopsy shows caseating granulomas.
oneliner: 41M + recent prison + cough, night sweats + PPD 14 mm + caseating granulomas → which macrophage cytokine drives granuloma formation?
ask: Release of which cytokine by infected macrophages most directly drives the T-cell response that forms these granulomas?

whyNot.A: Drives **Th2** differentiation and IgE class switching; opposes the Th1 response
whyNot.B: Promotes **eosinophil** growth and IgA switching, not granulomas
whyNot.C: Supports **early lymphocyte development**, not the response to a macrophage infection

answer: IL-12 from macrophages drives Th1 cells to make IFN-gamma
why: Infected macrophages release **IL-12**, which pushes CD4 cells to become **Th1** and activates NK cells. They make **interferon-gamma**, which activates macrophages to kill mycobacteria and form **granulomas**.
chain: Th1 and NK cells release IFN-gamma

idea.rule: IL-12 → IFN-gamma → macrophage activation is the key loop for containing intracellular organisms.
also: IL-12 receptor or IFN-gamma receptor defects cause disseminated atypical mycobacterial disease
Anti-TNF drugs can reactivate latent TB by breaking down granulomas
Same loop protects against Salmonella and fungi

stem: A 29-year-old woman who works as a nurse has a firm, raised, 25 mm area at the site of an intradermal purified protein derivative injection 48 hours ago. There is no blistering, and she has no symptoms.
oneliner: 29F + 25 mm firm induration 48 h after intradermal PPD, no blisters → which cell makes up most of the induration?
ask: Which cell type forms the bulk of the infiltrate in this skin reaction?

options.B: Macrophages recruited by memory CD4+ T cells

whyNot.A: Induration is not antibody-driven and **peaks at 48 to 72 hours**, not within minutes
whyNot.C: They are important in **contact dermatitis** (Ni, poison ivy), but not the bulk here
whyNot.D: Typical of **type I and parasitic** reactions
whyNot.E: Seen in **early** inflammation and bacterial infection, not a 48-hour delayed reaction

answer: Delayed-type reaction: memory Th1 cells recruit macrophages
why: Prior exposure left **memory CD4+ Th1 cells** in the skin. They release **IFN-gamma and cytokines** that recruit and activate **macrophages**, causing the firm induration.
chain: Prior TB exposure leaves memory CD4+ cells

idea.rule: Delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity is T-cell and macrophage mediated, with no antibody involved.
also: Other type IV: contact dermatitis, granulomas, graft rejection
Induration, not erythema, is the measured quantity
Anergy (e.g. advanced HIV) can give false negatives

stem: A 78-year-old man with an indwelling urinary catheter is brought in confused. Temperature is 35.6 C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 82/44 mm Hg despite 3 L of saline, and his hands are warm. Urine is cloudy with many white cells. A pulmonary artery catheter shows cardiac output 8.2 L/min, wedge pressure 8 mm Hg and systemic vascular resistance 450 dyn·s/cm5. Hemoglobin is stable at 13 g/dL, troponin is normal, the ECG is unchanged, and the neck veins are flat.
oneliner: 78M + catheter, cloudy urine + confused, T 35.6, HR 118, BP 82/44 after 3 L fluid, warm hands + CO high, wedge low-normal, SVR low + stable Hb, normal troponin → mechanism of hypotension?
ask: Which of the following best explains his low blood pressure?

options.B: Intravascular volume lost to occult bleeding
options.C: Pump failure from a silent myocardial infarction
options.D: Obstruction of the right ventricular outflow by a massive pulmonary embolus
options.E: Slowed contractility and heart rate from hypothyroidism

whyNot.B: Bleeding gives **low output and high resistance with cold hands**; his Hb is stable and CO is high
whyNot.C: **Troponin and ECG are normal**; cardiogenic shock has low output and high wedge pressure
whyNot.D: Would give **raised neck veins** and low output; his neck veins are flat

answer: Distributive (septic) shock: vasodilation lowers SVR with high cardiac output
why: A urinary source plus **low SVR, high cardiac output, low wedge pressure and warm hands** is **distributive shock**. Cytokines (TNF, IL-1) and **nitric oxide** relax arterioles, so pressure falls despite a high output.
chain: Bacterial toxins trigger TNF and IL-1 release

idea.rule: Distributive shock = low SVR with high CO; hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock = low CO.
also: Anaphylactic shock: histamine-driven vasodilation
Neurogenic shock: lost sympathetic tone (often with bradycardia)
Adrenal crisis can also present as low-SVR shock
Contrast: hypovolemic (low CO, high SVR, low wedge) and cardiogenic (low CO, high SVR, high wedge)

stem: A 29-year-old man has had a sudden onset of fever of 39.6 C, severe muscle aches and a runny nose for one day. He is shivering and under blankets and his hands and feet feel cool. He takes no medications and has not sweated yet.
oneliner: 29M + abrupt fever 39.6 + myalgia + runny nose + shivering under blankets, cool hands + no sweating + no drugs → why chills?
ask: Which event most directly accounts for his shivering?

options.E: A raised hypothalamic temperature set point

whyNot.A: The picture is a **systemic febrile illness** and does not require brain infection; no confusion or neck stiffness
whyNot.B: **Salicylate toxicity**: hyperthermia with sweating, not chills; he takes no drugs
whyNot.C: **Anticholinergic toxicity**: hot, flushed, dry skin and dilated pupils from a drug; he **takes no medications**
whyNot.D: **Thyroid storm**: tachycardia, tremor and goiter, not myalgia and rhinorrhea

answer: Cytokines and PGE2 raise the set point, so he shivers to reach it
why: Viral infection releases **IL-1, IL-6 and TNF**, which raise **PGE2** in the hypothalamus. The **set point rises**, so the body feels cold and **shivers and vasoconstricts** until core temperature reaches the new level.
chain: Fever; sweating when the set point falls

idea.rule: Fever is a raised set point (chills while rising), not a failure of heat loss.
also: Antipyretics block COX and so PGE2
Hyperthermia (heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia) has a normal set point
Defervescence brings sweating

stem: A 60-year-old man has fever, tachycardia and blood pressure 82/50 mm Hg after emergency surgery for a perforated diverticulum. Blood cultures grow Escherichia coli. His serum shows markedly raised TNF-alpha, IL-1 and IL-6.
oneliner: 60M + gram-negative sepsis after perforated diverticulum + fever, hypotension + high TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6 → which transcription factor links receptor to cytokines?
ask: Which transcription factor links toll-like receptor 4 signaling in his macrophages to this cytokine surge?

whyNot.B: **NFAT** is switched on by calcineurin in T cells and drives IL-2
whyNot.C: **STAT1** follows the interferon-gamma receptor, not TLR4
whyNot.D: **CREB** responds to cAMP signaling, not to LPS
whyNot.E: The **glucocorticoid receptor** switches these cytokines off; here they are **raised**

why: **Lipid A** of LPS binds **CD14 and TLR4** on macrophages. The adaptor pathway frees **NF-kB**, which enters the nucleus and switches on **TNF-alpha, IL-1 and IL-6**.
chain: E. coli enters blood from the perforated bowel
LPS (lipid A) engages CD14 and TLR4
NF-kB drives TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6 genes

idea.rule: TLR signals converge on NF-kB, the master switch for inflammatory cytokine genes.
also: TLR2 senses gram-positive peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acid
TLR3 senses viral double-stranded RNA
TLR5 senses flagellin
TLR9 senses unmethylated CpG DNA

stem: A 33-year-old man has had many unprotected exposures to partners with HIV but remains uninfected. His T cells and macrophages have normal CD4. Genetic testing shows he is homozygous for a 32-base-pair deletion in a surface protein gene, so his cells cannot support entry by the commonest transmitted strains.
oneliner: 33M + repeated HIV exposure but never infected + normal CD4 + homozygous 32-base-pair deletion in a surface protein gene → which molecule does HIV need besides CD4?
ask: Besides CD4, which cell-surface molecule do the commonly transmitted HIV strains need, and he lacks?

whyNot.B: **CD21** is the receptor for **Epstein-Barr virus** on B cells
whyNot.D: **CD40L** is a T-cell help molecule, not a viral entry receptor
whyNot.E: **Class I MHC** is on all cells, so it cannot explain why only **his** cells resist entry

why: **gp120** binds **CD4**, which exposes a site for a **chemokine co-receptor**: **CCR5** early in infection, **CXCR4** later. Then **gp41** drives **membrane fusion**. A **CCR5 delta-32 homozygote** is largely resistant.

idea.rule: HIV needs two receptors: CD4 first, a chemokine receptor second.
also: Maraviroc blocks CCR5
Enfuvirtide blocks gp41 fusion
CCR5 delta-32 homozygotes are protected; heterozygotes progress slowly
Epstein-Barr virus uses CD21, rhinovirus uses ICAM-1

stem: A 58-year-old man with an obstructing kidney stone has fever, flank pain and warm skin, and his blood pressure falls to 76/42 mm Hg. He has no rash. Blood cultures grow a gram-negative rod that ferments lactose.
oneliner: 58M + obstructing stone + fever, flank pain + warm skin + BP 76/42 + no rash + lactose-fermenting GNR in blood → how does the bacterium drop his pressure?
ask: Which mechanism best explains his hypotension?

options.A: Lipid A binds TLR4 on macrophages, releasing TNF-alpha and IL-1
options.B: O antigen forms immune complexes with IgG that deposit in vessel walls
options.C: Fimbriae bind the urothelium and trigger mast-cell histamine release
options.D: A secreted superantigen cross-links MHC class II and T-cell receptors
options.E: Peptidoglycan with teichoic acid binds TLR2 on macrophages

whyNot.B: Immune-complex disease takes **1 to 2 weeks**; his shock came with an acute infection
whyNot.C: Fimbriae mediate **adherence**; mast-cell release would bring hives or wheeze, and he has **no rash**
whyNot.D: Superantigen shock is a **gram-positive** toxin syndrome with a **rash**; he has a gram-negative rod and no rash
whyNot.E: Teichoic acid is a **gram-positive** wall component; his organism is a **gram-negative rod**

answer: Lipid A (endotoxin) of LPS activating TLR4/CD14 on macrophages → TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6 → vasodilation
why: The outer membrane of a gram-negative rod carries **LPS**. Its **lipid A** is the endotoxin: with **CD14 and TLR4** on macrophages it drives **TNF-alpha, IL-1 and IL-6** and **nitric oxide**, giving **warm, vasodilated shock**. The **O antigen** is the variable outer sugar chain used for **serotyping**, not the toxic part.
chain: LPS lipid A binds LBP and CD14
TLR4 signals through NF-κB in macrophages
TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6 and inducible NO synthase
Vasodilation and capillary leak → warm shock

idea.rule: LPS: lipid A = toxin (TLR4); O antigen = serotype; capsule = antiphagocytic; fimbriae = adherence.
also: O157 in E coli O157:H7 names the O antigen; H names the flagellar antigen
Gram-positive walls signal through TLR2 (lipoteichoic acid)
Endotoxin also activates complement and the clotting cascade (DIC)
Superantigens (TSST-1) bind MHC II and TCR outside the groove

stem: A 55-year-old man has had 3 days of watery diarrhea and lower abdominal cramps that began 2 days after he returned from a business trip to Mexico. He has no fever and no blood in the stool. Stool microscopy shows no leukocytes and sigmoidoscopy is normal. Stool culture on MacConkey agar grows pink colonies of a gram-negative rod.
oneliner: 55M + 3 days of watery diarrhea and cramps after trip to Mexico + no fever or blood + no fecal leukocytes + normal sigmoidoscopy + lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod → which enzyme and second messenger does the heat-stable toxin use?
ask: The organism's heat-stable enterotoxin causes diarrhea by acting through which of the following?

options.A: Adenylate cyclase with a rise in cAMP
options.B: Guanylate cyclase with a rise in cGMP
options.C: Phospholipase C with a rise in IP3 and calcium
options.D: Adenylate cyclase with a fall in cAMP
options.E: Phosphodiesterase with a fall in cGMP

whyNot.A: That is the pathway of the **heat-labile** toxin; the question asks about the **heat-stable** one
whyNot.C: A Gq pathway that neither toxin uses; his **watery diarrhea** is a secretory pattern
whyNot.D: A fall in cAMP would reduce secretion, but he has **profuse watery diarrhea**
whyNot.E: A fall in cGMP would reduce chloride secretion, but he has **watery diarrhea**

answer: Guanylate cyclase with a rise in cGMP
why: **Watery diarrhea after travel to Mexico** with **no fever, blood or leukocytes** and a **lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod** is enterotoxigenic E. coli. The heat-stable toxin activates **guanylate cyclase C**, raising **cGMP** in enterocytes, which drives chloride and water secretion.
chain: ETEC attaches to small-bowel enterocytes with pili
The heat-stable toxin binds guanylate cyclase C
CFTR opens; chloride and water secretion rise while NaCl absorption falls
Watery diarrhea with no blood or leukocytes

idea.rule: Secretory diarrhea toxins work by raising cyclic nucleotides in enterocytes.
also: Heat-labile toxin of ETEC: raises cAMP, like cholera toxin
Cholera toxin: ADP-ribosylates Gs, locking adenylate cyclase on
Both ETEC toxins give watery stool without leukocytes
Linaclotide treats constipation by activating the same guanylate cyclase C, raising cGMP
